2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Sugarcane is known for its thick, juicy stem, which is crushed to extract juice for sugar production or chewed directly.
solution: Think about what a sugarcane stalk looks like.
It is a long, thick, jointed part that grows upwards from the ground.
This upright, main body of the plant that bears leaves is the stem.
The sweet juice comes from this particular part of the plant.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: Most leaves on a healthy plant are what color?
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Healthy leaves are typically green due to the presence of chlorophyll, a pigment essential for making food.
solution: Look at the plants and trees in your garden or outside.
Observe the color of their leaves.
The most common color for healthy leaves is green.
This green color helps them make food from sunlight.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: Besides turning into fruits, what is another important purpose of a flower for the plant?
options: To hold the plant in the soil
To make food for the plant
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Flowers often have bright colors and pleasant smells to attract pollinators like bees, which are necessary for the formation of seeds and fruits.
solution: Recall what happens to flowers after they bloom.
They eventually turn into fruits, but something needs to happen for that.
Flowers are usually colorful and sometimes fragrant, which attracts insects like bees.
These insects help in carrying pollen, a process called pollination, which is vital for new seeds and fruits.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: Which of these parts is usually NOT seen above the ground?
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Roots typically grow beneath the soil, anchoring the plant and absorbing nutrients, while other parts are usually visible above ground.
solution: Think about the different parts of a plant you can easily see.
Flowers are bright and visible, stems stand tall, and leaves are usually green and visible.
The part that goes deep into the soil for support and water is not normally seen.
This hidden part is the root.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: Fruits provide us with essential things for our health. What do they contain that can grow a new plant?
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Fruits contain seeds, which are the reproductive part of the plant and, when planted under proper conditions, can germinate and grow into new plants.
solution: Think about what you do if you want to grow a new fruit tree.
You would take a part from the fruit and plant it.
While fruits have sugar, water, and vitamins, the part that can grow a new plant is the seed.
Seeds are designed to develop into new plants.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: Which part of a big tree is used to make wooden furniture like tables and chairs?
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: The strong, woody part of a large tree known as the trunk (which is its main stem) provides the timber used for making furniture.
solution: Think about what wooden furniture is made from.
It is made from wood.
Where does the hard, strong wood come from on a large tree?
The thick, central part that stands tall and supports the branches is called the trunk, which is a type of stem. This is where the useful wood comes from.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: A plant needs sunlight, water, and ______ to grow well.
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Soil provides a stable anchor for the roots and contains essential nutrients that plants absorb, along with water, sunlight, and air, to grow well.
solution: Recall what you need to put a seed into to help it grow.
You wouldn't put it in stones, air, or toys.
Plants need something for their roots to hold onto and get food from.
That 'something' is soil, which also provides water and nutrients.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: The juicy part of a mango that we eat is its ______.
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: A mango is a fleshy, edible fruit that develops from the flower of the mango tree and contains a single large seed.
solution: Think about how we classify edible parts of plants.
Is a mango a leaf, root, or stem? No.
We know that flowers develop into fruits after pollination.
The sweet, juicy, and edible part that grows from the mango tree and contains a seed is its fruit.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: When a seed sprouts, which part usually comes out first from the seed and grows downwards?
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: The root (radicle) is typically the first part to emerge from a germinating seed, growing downwards to anchor the plant and absorb water and nutrients.
solution: Imagine planting a small seed in the soil.
Before any green shoots appear above ground, the tiny plant needs water to grow.
The first part that pushes downwards into the soil is responsible for absorbing water and holding the plant.
This initial part is the root.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: Which two parts of a plant are most important for making new baby plants (reproduction)?
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Flowers contain the reproductive structures and develop into fruits, which protect the seeds necessary for the growth of new plants.
solution: Think about how new plants are created.
New plants grow from seeds.
Where are seeds found? Inside fruits.
And what develops into a fruit? A flower. So, flowers and fruits (which contain seeds) are crucial for making new plants.

2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.question: The green leafy part of a coriander plant that we use in cooking is its ______.
2::The World Around Us::plants-and-their.explanation: Coriander is a herb, and its fresh green, flat parts are the leaves, which are widely used as a flavoring in many dishes.
solution: Think about what fresh coriander looks like when you buy it.
It has small, delicate, green, flat parts.
These are the parts that are chopped and added to food for flavor and garnish.
These green, flat parts are clearly the leaves of the coriander plant.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home of a dog called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A kennel is a small shelter built specifically for dogs to live in.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where do birds usually build their homes to lay eggs?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Birds build nests in trees or other safe places to lay their eggs and raise their young.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A lion lives in a __________________.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A den is a wild animal's lair or dwelling place, and lions often live in dens.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal lives in a stable?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A stable is a building where horses are kept and cared for.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where would you most likely find a spider making its home?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Spiders spin webs to catch insects for food and also as a place to live.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home of a cow called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Cows are typically kept in a shed or a barn on a farm.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which of these animals makes a hive for its home?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Bees live together in a colony inside a structure called a hive.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home of a pig called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A sty is a pen or enclosure for pigs.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A rabbit digs a hole in the ground to live in. What is this home called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A burrow is a hole or tunnel dug by an animal, such as a rabbit, as a dwelling.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where do fish live?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Fish are aquatic animals and live in water, like rivers, ponds, and oceans.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Ants live in big communities underground in a home called a/an _____________.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: An anthill is a mound of earth, sand, or leaves built by ants as their nest.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A hen lives in a ___________.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A chicken coop is a house or enclosure where chickens are kept.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal typically lives in a hole in the ground or under rocks?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Snakes often live in holes in the ground, under rocks, or in logs for shelter.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A bear often lives in a large natural shelter like a cave, which can also be called a ____________.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A den is a natural hollow or shelter, often used by wild animals like bears for hibernation or raising young.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal's home is usually found high up in trees?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Monkeys are arboreal animals, meaning they live in trees for shelter and food.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which of these statements about animal homes is TRUE?
options: A horse lives in a sty.
A cow lives in a shed.
A rabbit lives in a kennel.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A cow lives in a shed or barn. Horses live in stables, birds build nests, and rabbits live in burrows.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home for sheep called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Sheep are kept in an enclosure called a pen.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: An animal that lives in a burrow is a/an _____________.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Rabbits are well-known for digging burrows in the ground to live in.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where would you find a squirrel's nest?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Squirrels build their nests, called dreys, high up in trees.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which pair of animal and home is INCORRECT?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Spiders spin webs, not nests. Dogs live in kennels, bees in hives, and lions in dens.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Some animals live in holes they dig in the ground to stay safe. What are these holes generally called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Burrows are holes or tunnels dug by animals in the ground to live in or for shelter.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home of a mouse often called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Mice typically live in small holes or cracks, often within walls or underground.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: If you see a lot of stored honey, what animal's home is nearby?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Bees store honey in their hives, which are their homes.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which of these animals builds its home using mud and twigs?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Many birds build nests using materials like mud, twigs, and leaves.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where do penguins live?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Penguins live in very cold regions, like Antarctica, building nests on land or ice.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What kind of home protects a snail?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Snails carry their homes, which are shells, on their backs for protection.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal creates a home that is known for its intricate tunnels and chambers?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Anthills are complex structures with many tunnels and chambers where ants live and store food.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A farmer keeps his chickens in a _______________.
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A coop is a cage or enclosure for poultry, especially chickens.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal would NOT live in a home made mostly of branches and leaves?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Spiders spin webs, while birds, monkeys, and squirrels often build nests or live in trees using branches and leaves.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which home is built by an animal primarily for trapping food?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A spider's web is spun not only as a home but also primarily to catch insects for food.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home of a bird called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Birds construct nests, often in trees, using materials like twigs and leaves, to lay eggs and raise their young.
solution: Recall common animals and their homes.
Think about where birds live.
Birds gather twigs and leaves to build their homes.
This home, typically found in trees, is called a nest.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where does a dog usually live?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A kennel is a specially built shelter, usually outdoors, designed to house dogs.
solution: Consider the common pet animal, a dog.
Dogs can live inside houses, but specific outdoor shelters are often built for them.
This dedicated shelter for a dog is known as a kennel.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal lives in a 'stable'?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A stable is a building specifically designed for housing horses, providing them with shelter and stalls.
solution: Identify the given animal home: 'stable'.
Recall which large domestic animal is commonly kept in a stable.
Horses are housed and cared for in stables.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: What is the home of a lion called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Lions typically live in a den or a lair, which is often a cave or a sheltered, secluded spot in the wild.
solution: Think about large wild animals like a lion.
Lions need a strong and safe place to live in the wild to rest and protect their young.
Their natural home is commonly referred to as a den or a lair.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Where do bees live and store their honey?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Bees construct intricate hives, either in natural locations like trees or in man-made boxes, where they live and produce honey.
solution: Identify the animal: bees.
Recall what bees are famous for making and where they store it.
Bees live together in a communal structure called a hive.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal makes its home in a 'coop'?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A coop is an enclosure or small house primarily used for keeping chickens and other poultry on a farm.
solution: Consider the animal home: 'coop'.
Think about farm animals that live in small, enclosed shelters for protection.
Chickens are commonly kept in a coop.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: An animal that loves to eat carrots and lives in a 'burrow' is a:
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Rabbits are well-known for their diet of carrots and for digging burrows, which are underground tunnels, for their homes.
solution: Read the clues provided: 'eats carrots' and 'lives in a burrow'.
A burrow is a hole or tunnel dug by an animal, usually in the ground.
Rabbits are famous for both digging burrows and eating carrots.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which of these animals lives in an 'anthill'?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: An anthill is a complex, visible structure built by a colony of ants, usually made of soil and sand, that serves as their home.
solution: Look at the name of the home: 'anthill'.
The name itself strongly suggests the animal that lives there.
An 'anthill' is the characteristic home of ants.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal spins a 'web' as its home to catch food?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Spiders are unique in their ability to spin intricate webs, which serve both as their home and a trap to catch insects for food.
solution: Read the clue: 'spins a web'.
Think about which small creature is famous for creating a silky web.
Spiders spin webs both as a place to live and as a way to hunt prey.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A 'cow shed' or 'barn' is the home for which farm animal?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Cows are typically kept in large shelters known as cow sheds or barns on farms, providing protection and space.
solution: Identify the given homes: 'cow shed' or 'barn'.
The term 'cow shed' directly indicates the animal.
Cows live in these shelters on farms for milking and protection.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal carries its home on its back?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A snail has a protective shell on its back that acts as its permanent, portable home and provides shelter when needed.
solution: Think about animals that are never separated from their homes.
Consider an animal whose home is an integral part of its body structure.
A snail's shell acts as its portable home and shield, carried on its back.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Why do animals build homes?
options: To stay safe and raise young
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Animals build homes primarily for protection from predators, harsh weather conditions, and to provide a secure environment for their offspring.
solution: Consider the most fundamental needs of animals in the wild.
Homes provide essential shelter from environmental elements like rain, sun, and cold.
Most importantly, homes offer safety from dangers and are crucial places for caring for and raising baby animals.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which of these homes is typically built by humans for domestic animals?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Nests, dens, and webs are natural structures built by wild animals, whereas a kennel is constructed by humans specifically for pet dogs.
solution: Analyze each option to determine its builder.
Nests (birds), Dens (lions/wolves), and Webs (spiders) are creations of the animals themselves.
A Kennel is a man-made structure specifically designed and built by people for domestic dogs.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: An animal that lives in a 'hole in the ground' and often hunts mice is called a:
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Foxes are known to live in underground burrows or dens (holes in the ground) and are skilled predators that hunt small animals like mice.
solution: Identify the clues given: 'lives in a hole in the ground' and 'hunts mice'.
Eliminate options that do not fit these characteristics: Horses live in stables, Bees in hives, Birds in nests.
Foxes live in dens (holes in the ground) and are known for preying on mice and other small creatures.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which home is usually made of twigs, leaves, and mud?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Birds meticulously gather and weave natural materials like twigs, leaves, grass, and mud to construct their sturdy nests.
solution: Think about homes built from natural, easily available materials found outdoors.
Consider which animal uses twigs, leaves, and mud to construct its shelter.
Birds use these specific materials to weave and build their nests.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: A 'fish tank' is a home for:
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A fish tank is a man-made container filled with water, serving as an artificial habitat to keep fish as pets.
solution: Read the name of the home: 'fish tank'.
The name itself directly tells you which animal is housed in it.
A fish tank is specifically designed as a home for fish.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which of these animals lives in a 'hole' in a tree trunk?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Squirrels often seek shelter and build their nests, called dreys, inside hollows or holes found in tree trunks or branches.
solution: Think about small animals that live in trees.
Consider which animal is known to store food in trees and often uses tree holes for shelter.
Squirrels are commonly found living in tree holes or building nests within trees.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: Which animal's home can be found underground in tunnels?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: Ants live in large colonies within complex systems of underground tunnels, often seen as an anthill on the surface.
solution: Consider animals that are known for living underground.
Think about which animals create extensive and organized tunnel systems.
Ants build large, interconnected underground networks as their homes and colonies.

2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.question: If a farmer builds a structure with strong fences and a roof to keep sheep safe, what is it most likely called?
2::The World Around Us::animals-and-thei.explanation: A 'pen' is a general term for an enclosed area, often with fences and a roof, used to keep farm animals like sheep or goats.
solution: Analyze the description: 'strong fences and a roof to keep sheep safe'.
Eliminate options that are specific to other animals: 'Stable' is for horses, 'Kennel' for dogs, 'Hive' for bees.
A 'pen' is the appropriate term for an enclosed space for livestock such as sheep.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Can we see the air around us?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air is invisible, which means we cannot see it with our eyes. We can only feel it when it moves.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What do all living things need to breathe?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: All living things, including humans, animals, and plants, need air to breathe and survive.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What is moving air called?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air that moves from one place to another is called wind.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: When you blow air into a balloon, what happens to it?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Blowing air into a balloon fills it up, making it expand and get bigger because air occupies space.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What helps clothes dry quickly after washing them?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Sunlight and moving air (wind) help water evaporate from clothes, making them dry faster.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Where can we find air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air is present everywhere around us, even though we cannot see it.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which of these tells us that air is present?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: We cannot see air, but we can feel it when it moves as wind.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What do plants need from the air to make their food?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide from the air along with sunlight and water to make their own food.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What is a gentle and pleasant moving air called?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: A light and gentle moving air is called a breeze.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What flies in the sky because of the wind?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Kites are designed to fly high in the sky when the wind pushes against them.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What comes out of vehicles and factories that makes the air dirty?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Vehicles and factories release smoke and harmful gases into the air, which makes it dirty and polluted.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: How does air help a sailboat move on water?
options: It pushes the boat from below
It pulls the boat with a string
It makes the water move faster
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Wind (moving air) pushes against the sails of a sailboat, helping it to move across the water.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What happens to a flat football when it is filled with air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: When a flat football is filled with air, the air takes up space inside it, making it firm and round, ready to be played with.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which of these activities helps keep the air clean?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Planting more trees helps to clean the air by absorbing harmful gases and releasing fresh air.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why is it bad to breathe dirty air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Dirty air contains harmful particles and gases that can cause breathing problems and other illnesses, making us sick.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: If you blow air into a paper bag, and then burst it, what makes the sound?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: When you burst a paper bag filled with air, the trapped air rushes out quickly, creating a sudden sound due to the rapid pressure change.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why do we feel hot on a very still day with no wind?
options: Wind helps to cool us down
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Wind helps to carry away the heat from our bodies and evaporate sweat, making us feel cooler. Without wind, the heat stays around us.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What do birds need to fly in the sky?
options: Air to push against their wings
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Birds use their wings to push against the air, which helps them to lift off and fly in the sky.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which statement is true about air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air takes up space, as shown when we inflate balloons or fill a bottle with air. It also has weight.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What is a very strong and destructive moving air called?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: A very strong wind that can cause damage is called a storm.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why do people in cities often wear masks or cover their mouths and noses?
options: To protect from dirty air and germs
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: People wear masks to protect themselves from breathing in dirty air, dust, smoke, and germs that can cause illness.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: If you put an 'empty' glass upside down into a bucket of water, why does the water not fill the glass completely?
options: Air is trapped inside the glass
There is a hole in the glass
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: The 'empty' glass is actually full of air. When you push it upside down into water, the trapped air prevents the water from filling the glass completely, showing that air occupies space.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: How do trees help in making the air clean and fresh for us?
options: They absorb water from the air
They take in bad air and give out good air
They make a lot of noise
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Trees absorb carbon dioxide (a 'bad' gas) from the air and release oxygen (a 'good' gas) that we breathe, thus making the air clean and fresh.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What would most likely happen if there was no air on Earth?
options: Living things could not breathe and survive
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air contains oxygen, which is essential for living things to breathe. Without air, life as we know it would not be possible on Earth.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: When you pump air into a bicycle tyre, what happens to the air inside the tyre?
options: It gets compressed and fills the tyre
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Pumping air into a tyre compresses the air, forcing more air into the fixed space, which makes the tyre hard and firm.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: You have two identical balloons. One is filled with air, and the other is empty (deflated). If you put them on a simple balance scale, which side would go down?
options: It depends on the color of the balloon
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: The air-filled balloon would make its side go down because air has weight, making the inflated balloon slightly heavier than the deflated one.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why is it important to have an air pump to fill the tyres of a bicycle or car?
options: To remove air from the tyres
To push a lot of air into a small space to make tyres firm
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: An air pump pushes and compresses air into the tyre, making it hard and firm enough to support the vehicle's weight. This shows air occupies space and can be compressed.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Imagine a world where there is no wind. Which of these would NOT be possible?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Kites need moving air (wind) to be able to fly and stay up in the sky. Without wind, a kite cannot fly.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why do factory chimneys release smoke high up into the air?
options: To make the sky look pretty
To make the smoke disappear quickly
To spread the pollution away from people on the ground
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Factories release smoke from tall chimneys so that the pollutants are released higher up and dispersed over a larger area, reducing immediate direct exposure to people on the ground, although it still pollutes the environment.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: If there was no air, what would happen to the sound of a drum?
options: It would not be heard at all
It would become a different sound
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Sound needs a medium like air to travel. If there was no air, the vibrations from the drum would not be able to reach our ears, and we would not hear any sound.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What is all around us, but we cannot see it?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air is an invisible mixture of gases that surrounds the Earth, essential for life.
solution: Think about what is present everywhere around us.
Consider things you can see (water, soil, toys) and things you cannot.
Air is something we cannot see but can feel its presence.
Therefore, air is all around us, but we cannot see it.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why do living things like humans and animals need air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: All living beings, including humans and animals, need air to breathe and stay alive.
solution: Recall what you do continuously to stay alive.
Think about what you take in when you inhale.
Humans and animals take in air to breathe.
Breathing is essential for all living things.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What happens when you blow air into a balloon?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: When you blow air into a balloon, the air fills the space inside, making the balloon expand and get bigger.
solution: Imagine a flat balloon.
When you blow air into it, you are putting air inside.
The air takes up space inside the balloon.
This causes the balloon to inflate and become bigger.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: When can you feel the air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: We can feel air when it moves, like a breeze on our skin or wind blowing.
solution: Think about when you feel something against your skin that you can't see.
If the air is still, you usually don't notice it much.
When air moves, it creates a feeling, like a gentle breeze or strong wind.
So, you can feel the air when it is moving.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What do we call fast-moving air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Moving air is called wind; a gentle wind is a breeze, and a very strong wind is a storm.
solution: Recall the different names for moving air.
A gentle movement of air is called a breeze.
A strong or fast movement of air is called wind.
A very strong, destructive wind often with rain is a storm. Therefore, fast-moving air is wind.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which of these shows that air has weight?
options: A kite flying in the sky.
A deflated balloon and an inflated balloon.
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: An inflated balloon is slightly heavier than a deflated one because the air inside it adds weight, demonstrating that air has weight.
solution: Think about the property 'air has weight.'
If air has weight, then something filled with air should be heavier than the same thing without air.
A kite flying shows air's force/movement, not weight directly. Smoke rising shows hot air is lighter than cold air.
An inflated balloon contains air, making it slightly heavier than an empty (deflated) balloon, proving air has weight.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: How does air help us with wet clothes?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Moving air helps to evaporate the water from wet clothes, making them dry faster.
solution: Think about what happens when you hang wet clothes outside.
The clothes become dry over time.
This drying process is helped by the moving air, or wind.
Therefore, air helps to dry wet clothes.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What makes the air dirty or polluted?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Smoke from vehicles contains harmful gases and particles that pollute the air, making it unhealthy to breathe.
solution: Consider what 'polluted' means - something harmful or dirty.
Plants, clean water, and fresh fruits are generally good for us and the environment.
Smoke from vehicles is known to be black and contain harmful substances.
This smoke released into the atmosphere makes the air dirty and unhealthy, which is air pollution.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What can we do to keep the air clean?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Trees help to clean the air by absorbing carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen, making them vital for clean air.
solution: Think about how air becomes polluted (e.g., smoke).
Consider what helps clean the air or prevent pollution.
Cutting trees, burning garbage, and driving cars more all contribute to air pollution.
Planting more trees helps because trees take in dirty air (carbon dioxide) and give out clean air (oxygen).

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Why does a fire need air to burn?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Fire needs oxygen from the air to sustain combustion and keep burning.
solution: Recall what happens if you cover a burning candle with a glass.
The flame goes out because it runs out of air.
The part of the air that fire needs to burn is oxygen.
So, fire needs air to provide oxygen to keep burning.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which of these devices uses moving air to work?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: A windmill uses the force of moving air (wind) to turn its blades and generate power.
solution: Think about how each option works.
A bicycle is powered by human legs.
A television uses electricity. A refrigerator uses electricity to cool things.
A windmill has large blades that spin when the wind (moving air) pushes them, showing it uses moving air to work.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What does air help birds and airplanes to do?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air provides the necessary lift and resistance for birds and airplanes to be able to fly.
solution: Think about where birds and airplanes are usually seen.
Both birds and airplanes move through the sky.
The movement in the sky is called flying.
Air is essential for them to fly.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Air is made up of many _____.
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Air is primarily a mixture of various gases, such as nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide.
solution: Recall what air is. Is it something you can hold like a solid? Or pour like a liquid?
Air is invisible and spreads out to fill any space.
This is a property of gases.
So, air is made up of many gases.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Breathing polluted air can make us _____.
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Polluted air contains harmful substances that can damage our lungs and cause respiratory problems, making us sick.
solution: Consider what happens when you are exposed to something unhealthy.
Polluted air has dirty particles and harmful gases.
If we breathe in these harmful things, it affects our body.
Breathing polluted air can lead to health problems and make us sick.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What is the usual smell of clean air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Clean air is generally odorless, meaning it has no particular smell.
solution: Think about how air usually smells when it is fresh and clean.
Does it smell like flowers, or something sweet, or smoke?
Clean air does not have any particular scent.
Therefore, clean air usually has no smell.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: If you fill an empty bottle with water, what did the water replace?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Even an 'empty' bottle is actually full of air, and when you add water, the water takes the place of the air.
solution: Imagine an 'empty' bottle. Is it truly empty?
No, it's filled with air.
When you pour water into it, the water occupies the space that the air was previously holding.
So, the water replaced the air inside the bottle.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which of these is NOT a source of air pollution?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Oxygen released by plants is essential for life and helps to keep the air clean, unlike smoke, dust, and burning garbage which pollute the air.
solution: Recall what causes air pollution (things that make air dirty or harmful).
Smoke from factories and burning garbage release harmful gases and particles.
Dust from construction sites also makes the air dirty.
Oxygen from plants is what we breathe and is vital for clean air, so it is NOT a source of pollution.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: What do we call moving air?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: Moving air is commonly known as wind.
solution: Think about the feeling of air moving past you.
What is the common term for this moving air?
It's not water, stone, or cloud.
Moving air is called wind.

2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.question: Which of these needs air to inflate and be used?
2::The World Around Us::air-around-us.explanation: A football is hollow and needs to be inflated with air to become firm and bouncy enough to play with.
solution: Consider each item and whether it needs air.
A brick, a book, and a spoon are solid objects and do not need air to be used.
A football, when deflated, is soft and flat.
To make a football round and bouncy for playing, you need to pump air into it, or inflate it.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What makes water turn into water vapour and go up into the sky?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The Sun's heat provides the energy for water to evaporate and turn into water vapour.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What are clouds mostly made of?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Clouds are formed when water vapour cools down and condenses into tiny water droplets or ice crystals.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: When water vapour cools down high up in the sky, what does it mainly form?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Cooling water vapour condenses to form tiny water droplets, which group together to make clouds.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What falls from the clouds when they become very heavy?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: When clouds are too heavy with water droplets, the water falls back to Earth as rain.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the continuous journey of water from the Earth to the sky and back again called?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle is the natural process where water constantly moves between Earth's surface and the atmosphere.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Which of these is NOT a natural source of water?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Rivers, lakes, and oceans are natural sources, while a tap is a man-made way to get water.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the process called when water changes into water vapour due to the sun's heat?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Evaporation is the process where liquid water turns into a gas (water vapour) and rises into the air.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: The process where water vapour turns back into tiny water droplets to form clouds is called:
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Condensation is when water vapour cools and changes back into liquid water droplets, forming clouds.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Where does the rainwater finally collect after falling on Earth?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: After rain falls, it flows into and collects in various water bodies like rivers, lakes, and oceans.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Why is the water cycle important for us?
options: It helps plants grow without water.
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle provides fresh water through rain, which is essential for all living things.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Which of these happens FIRST in the water cycle?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle begins when the sun heats up water on Earth, causing it to evaporate.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Which step usually comes AFTER evaporation in the water cycle?
options: Water vapour cools and forms clouds
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: After water evaporates and rises, it cools down and condenses to form clouds.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: When water turns into vapour, what form of water is it?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Water vapour is the gaseous form of water, which is invisible.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: If there was no sun, what would happen to the water cycle?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The sun's heat is necessary for evaporation, so without it, water would not turn into vapour.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Can we easily see water vapour in the air?
options: Yes, it looks like white smoke
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Water vapour is a clear, invisible gas, unlike visible clouds which are tiny water droplets.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What happens to water vapour as it rises high up in the sky?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: As water vapour rises higher into the atmosphere, the temperature drops and it gets colder.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: The water we drink today has been part of the water cycle for a very long time, being recycled again and again. Is this statement True or False?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle constantly recycles Earth's water, so the same water has been around for millions of years.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What does rain help to fill?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Rain is crucial for refilling natural water bodies like rivers, lakes, and ponds.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Water heats up, turns into vapour, then __________, then forms rain. What is the missing step?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: After water evaporates, the vapour cools down and condenses to form clouds, which then release rain.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the primary source of energy for the water cycle?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The Sun's energy drives the entire water cycle by heating water and causing evaporation.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: If a puddle dries up on a sunny day, which part of the water cycle is mainly happening?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: When a puddle dries up, the water turns into vapour and rises into the air due to the sun's heat, which is evaporation.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Why do clouds sometimes look white and fluffy?
options: They are made of tiny water droplets reflecting sunlight.
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Clouds appear white because the tiny water droplets scatter all colors of sunlight equally.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is 'precipitation' in simple terms?
options: Water falling from the sky (like rain)
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Precipitation is any form of water that falls from the clouds to the Earth's surface, like rain, snow, or hail.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Which of these would mostly likely be 'collection' areas for rainwater?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Oceans and ponds are large bodies of water where rainwater naturally collects and accumulates.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: The same water is used over and over again on Earth because of which process?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle ensures that water is continuously recycled and reused across the Earth.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: The Sun helps in which step of the water cycle?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The Sun's heat is essential for the evaporation process, where water turns into vapour.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: After evaporation, where does the water vapor go?
options: It goes up into the atmosphere.
It goes into the rivers directly.
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Evaporated water vapour rises high up into the Earth's atmosphere.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the main difference between water vapor and a cloud?
options: Water vapor is visible, a cloud is not.
Water vapor is liquid, a cloud is gas.
Water vapor is an invisible gas, a cloud is visible tiny water droplets.
Water vapor is hot, a cloud is cold.
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Water vapor is an invisible gas, while a cloud is made of visible tiny water droplets or ice crystals.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is fog an example of, relating to the water cycle?
options: Condensation (water droplets in the air near the ground)
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Fog is essentially a cloud that forms near the ground when water vapour condenses into tiny droplets.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Besides filling water bodies, what else does rain help?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Rain provides essential water for plants, helping them to grow and thrive.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: When clouds get too heavy, what falls from the sky?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: When clouds accumulate too much water, the water falls back to Earth in the form of rain, snow, or hail, a process called precipitation.
solution: Imagine a big, dark cloud full of water.
What happens when these clouds can no longer hold all the water?
The water comes down from the sky.
We call this falling water 'rain'.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Which of these is the correct order for parts of the water cycle?
options: Sun heats Ocean water → Clouds form → Rain falls
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The sun heats water in oceans, causing evaporation. This water vapour forms clouds (condensation), and then falls as rain (precipitation).
solution: Think about where the water cycle usually begins. It starts with the sun's heat.
The sun heats water bodies like oceans, making water go up (evaporation).
This water vapour forms clouds high in the sky (condensation).
Finally, the clouds release water as rain (precipitation).

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Why is the water cycle important for us and all living things?
options: It helps plants grow by providing water
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle continuously provides fresh water in the form of rain, which is essential for the survival and growth of all living organisms, including plants.
solution: What does the water cycle give us? It gives us rain.
What do plants need to grow big and strong?
They need water to live and grow.
Rainwater from the water cycle helps all plants thrive.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the process called when water turns into invisible water vapour and rises into the air?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Evaporation is the process where liquid water absorbs heat energy and changes into a gas (water vapour), rising into the atmosphere.
solution: Remember what happens when the sun heats a puddle of water.
The water seems to disappear into the air, becoming invisible.
This specific change from liquid water to water vapour is called evaporation.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: When water vapour in the sky cools down and changes back into tiny water droplets to form clouds, what is this process called?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Condensation is the process where water vapour loses heat, cools, and changes back into liquid water droplets or ice crystals, forming clouds.
solution: Think about what happens after water vapour goes up high into the cooler air.
When warm water vapour gets cold, it changes back into tiny liquid water drops.
This change from an invisible gas (vapour) to visible liquid droplets (clouds) is called condensation.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: After rain falls on the land, where does much of the water eventually go?
options: It stays on the surface forever
It flows into rivers, lakes, and oceans or sinks into the ground
It floats back up into the sky immediately
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: After precipitation, rainwater either flows over the land as runoff to collect in bodies of water or seeps into the ground to become groundwater, a stage known as collection.
solution: Once rain falls on the ground, observe where it goes.
It doesn't just stay where it lands forever; it moves.
Water naturally flows downhill and gathers in larger water bodies.
It can also soak into the soil, becoming underground water, or flow into rivers, lakes, and oceans.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Which of these provides the most heat for the water cycle to begin and continue?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The Sun is the primary and most powerful source of energy that drives the entire water cycle by causing evaporation of water.
solution: Think about what gives the whole Earth heat and light.
A bonfire, heater, or lamp give heat, but only to a small area.
The Sun is the biggest natural source of heat for our planet.
Its heat is what makes water warm up and evaporate, starting the water cycle.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What do many tiny water droplets join together to make in the sky?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: When countless tiny water droplets, formed from condensed water vapour, gather together high in the atmosphere, they become visible as clouds.
solution: Remember the tiny water droplets formed when water vapour cools down.
When many, many of these tiny drops come together and float high up in the sky.
They become big enough for us to see clearly.
These large groups of tiny drops are what we call clouds.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the most common form of precipitation we usually see in India?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Rain is the most common and widespread form of precipitation experienced in most parts of India, especially relevant for a Class 2 student's understanding.
solution: Think about what usually falls from the sky when clouds are heavy with water.
Do we often see snow in most parts of India? Not usually, only in specific cold regions.
Hail is less common than rain. Mist is tiny droplets but doesn't 'fall' like rain.
Rain is what we experience most frequently from clouds.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Evaporation → Condensation → ______ → Collection. What is the missing step in this sequence of the water cycle?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The four main stages of the water cycle are evaporation (water goes up), condensation (clouds form), precipitation (water falls down), and collection (water gathers).
solution: Recall the key stages of the water cycle in order.
First, water goes up as vapour (evaporation).
Then, the vapour cools and forms clouds (condensation).
Next, water falls down from the clouds. What is that called?
That stage is called precipitation, which is followed by water gathering (collection).

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: When water becomes water vapour and goes up into the air, what state of water is it?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Water vapour is the gaseous state of water, which is invisible and rises into the atmosphere during evaporation.
solution: Water can be in different forms: solid (ice), liquid (drinking water), or gas (vapour/steam).
When water turns into water vapour and rises, it becomes invisible.
This invisible form of water is known as a gas.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Where does the water from rain eventually gather to complete the cycle?
options: In big water bodies like oceans, lakes, and rivers
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: After falling as rain, water flows over land or seeps into the ground, eventually collecting in larger bodies of water such as rivers, lakes, and oceans, ready to evaporate again.
solution: After it rains, where do you see puddles and streams flowing?
These small streams usually flow towards bigger ones.
All the water eventually finds its way to large bodies of water.
These large bodies are oceans, lakes, and rivers, where the collection stage happens.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: How do plants help in the water cycle?
options: They stop the rain from falling
They take in water from the ground and release some as vapour
They only use water for themselves and don't contribute
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Plants absorb water from the soil through their roots and release water vapour into the atmosphere through their leaves, a process called transpiration, contributing to cloud formation.
solution: Think about what plants do with water from the soil.
They absorb water through their roots to grow.
Some of this water comes out from their leaves as invisible vapour into the air.
This process adds water vapour to the atmosphere, just like evaporation from water bodies.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the main energy source that powers the entire water cycle?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The sun's energy provides the heat necessary for evaporation, which is the starting and driving force of the water cycle.
solution: What makes water warm up and turn into vapour?
What gives heat to our entire planet?
The Sun is the biggest source of heat and energy for Earth.
Therefore, the Sun is what makes the water cycle work.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: What is the main role of clouds in the water cycle?
options: To hold water vapour and then release it as rain
To make pretty shapes in the sky
To carry birds to faraway places
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: Clouds are formed from condensed water vapour and are crucial for transporting and releasing water back to Earth as precipitation.
solution: What do clouds become after they are formed from water vapour?
They gather more and more water droplets, getting bigger and heavier.
What happens when they get very heavy and cold?
They release the water they are holding, causing rain to fall.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: If there was no sun, what would happen to the water cycle on Earth?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The sun's heat is absolutely essential for evaporation, the first step of the water cycle. Without the sun, water would not evaporate, and the entire cycle would cease.
solution: Remember what starts the water cycle – it's the sun's heat.
The sun's heat causes water to turn into vapour and rise (evaporation).
If there is no sun, there would be no heat to make water evaporate.
Without evaporation, the water cycle cannot begin or continue, so it would stop.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: When wet clothes dry in the sun, which part of the water cycle is primarily happening?
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The sun's heat causes the water in the wet clothes to turn into invisible water vapour and rise into the air, which is the process of evaporation.
solution: Think about what happens when you hang wet clothes in the sun.
The clothes become dry, meaning the water has gone somewhere.
The water doesn't fall as rain or form clouds on your clothes.
The heat from the sun makes the liquid water turn into invisible vapour and go into the air. This change is evaporation.

2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.question: Why is the continuous movement of water called the 'water cycle'?
options: Because it goes around and around in a continuous path
Because it makes a perfect circle shape in the sky
Because it is a game that water plays
2::The World Around Us::water-cycle.explanation: The water cycle is called a 'cycle' because water continuously moves in a closed loop, changing states and locations as it travels from Earth to the atmosphere and back again.
solution: Think about what the word 'cycle' means (like a bicycle wheel).
A cycle means something that goes round and round or repeats.
The water goes from the Earth to the sky, and then back to the Earth, always moving in a continuous path.
This continuous, repeating movement is why it's called a cycle.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these is a healthy food that helps you grow strong?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Milk is a healthy food rich in calcium, which is very important for strong bones and teeth, helping children grow well.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these foods should you eat only sometimes, as it's not very healthy?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: A burger is often considered junk food because it contains a lot of oil, salt, and unhealthy fats, which are not good for daily consumption.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Why do we need to eat food every day?
options: To get energy to play and study
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Food gives our body the energy it needs to do all our daily activities like playing, studying, running, and thinking.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: What should you always do before eating your food?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Washing your hands before eating removes germs and dirt, which helps prevent you from getting sick.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these foods do we get from a plant?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Rice grains grow on paddy plants in fields, making it a food item we get from plants.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Eating a lot of fruits and vegetables helps you to:
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Fruits and vegetables are packed with vitamins and minerals that boost your immune system, helping your body fight off common illnesses and stay healthy.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: How many glasses of water should a child drink every day?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Drinking 6-8 glasses of water daily is important for children to stay hydrated, help their body function well, and keep them active.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which food item is a good source of protein for strong muscles?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Dal, or lentils, is a rich source of plant-based protein, which is essential for building and repairing muscles and helping you grow strong.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these is a green leafy vegetable?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Spinach is a green leafy vegetable that is very healthy and full of iron, making it good for your blood.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: If you eat too many sweets and chocolates, what might happen to your teeth?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Sugary foods like sweets and chocolates can cause tooth decay and cavities if eaten too often and teeth are not brushed properly.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Chapati and rice give us a lot of energy to run and play. Which type of food are they?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Chapati and rice are rich in carbohydrates, which are the main source of energy for our body, helping us to be active and play.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: What should you do with food that is left on your plate?
options: Finish it or save it for later if possible
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: We should never waste food because many people in the world do not have enough to eat. It's important to eat what you take or save leftovers safely.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: From which of these do we get oil for cooking?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Many cooking oils, like sunflower oil, are extracted from the seeds of plants such as the sunflower plant.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Why is it important to eat a variety of different healthy foods every day?
options: To make your plate look colourful
To get all the nutrients your body needs
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Eating different types of healthy foods ensures your body receives all the essential vitamins, minerals, proteins, and carbohydrates it needs to grow, stay healthy, and have energy.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these foods do we get from animals?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Eggs are laid by birds like hens, making them a food product that comes from animals.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Why is it bad to eat food from street vendors that looks uncovered?
options: It might have germs and make you sick
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Uncovered food can easily collect dust, flies, and germs from the air, which can cause stomach problems and illness when eaten.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these is a pulse (dal)?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Moong dal is a type of lentil, or pulse, which is commonly eaten in India and is a good source of protein.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these is the healthiest drink for your body?
options: Packed fruit juice with added sugar
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Water is the best drink for your body as it has no sugar or artificial ingredients, keeping you hydrated and healthy.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: If you skip your breakfast, how might you feel during your morning classes?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Breakfast is an important meal that provides energy after a long night. Skipping it can make you feel hungry, tired, and unable to focus on your studies.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these is a fruit?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: A banana is a yellow, sweet fruit that is easy to peel and is packed with energy.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: A typical healthy Indian meal usually includes:
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: A traditional Indian meal is balanced with proteins from dal, carbohydrates from rice or chapati, and vitamins/minerals from vegetables, making it a healthy choice.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Eating too much junk food regularly can make you:
options: Feel tired and gain unhealthy weight
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Junk food is high in unhealthy fats and sugar but low in essential nutrients. Eating it too often can lead to feeling sluggish, gaining unhealthy weight, and other health problems.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Besides food, what else do we need to drink to live and stay healthy?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Water is vital for all life processes in our body; we cannot live long without drinking enough water every day.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Why should you chew your food slowly and properly?
options: To make your meal last longer
To help your stomach digest it easily
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Chewing food properly breaks it down into smaller pieces, which makes it easier for your stomach to digest and absorb nutrients.

2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.subject: The World Around Us
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.question: Which of these is a root vegetable?
2::The World Around Us::healthy-food.explanation: Carrots grow underground and are the root part of the plant, known for being good for eyesight.
